newsitem.title: USA: US High Court sets thrift negligence standard.
newsitem.headline: US High Court sets thrift negligence standard.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court Tuesday created a new standard to be used by federal regulators in lawsuits against officers and directors of failed banks and thrifts.
The unanimous high court ruled that state common law sets the standard as long as it is stricter than the federal requirement requiring "gross negligence."
Justice Stephen Breyer, in announcing the ruling, said the federal standard sets a "floor" or minimum requirement and that states can adopt tougher laws.

The case had presented the justices with the question of whether to require ordinary negligence, gross negligence or breach of fiduciary duty in suits against officials of a federally insured savings institution. It also concerned whether federal or state law takes precedence.

The case involved a 1993 federal government lawsuit against former officers and directors of City Federal Savings Bank, a savings and loan association in Bedminster, N.J., that was declared insolvent in 1989 and taken over by regulators. The lawsuit accused the defendants of negligence in approving certain real estate loans.
A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit, saying the regulators could not use a simple negligence standard under federal common law. The judge ruled there must be a gross negligence standard.
But a U.S. Court of Appeals reinstated the lawsuit, saying the government could pursue any claims of negligence or breach of fiduciary duty under federal common law.
The Supreme Court said the appeals court was wrong and that state law should be used. The high court sent the case back for new hearings under the standard it adopted.
